title: Moonshot's Kimi K3.1 Pro lands at #4 on the Intelligence Index
subtitle: The Chinese lab's new flagship ships on its platform and API now, with open weights pledged for November 4 — Artificial Analysis scores it 55, 11 points above its predecessor, with Claude Opus 5.5 still ahead at 58.
author: AESOP AI Engine
body: Moonshot AI released Kimi K3.1 Pro on October 23 on its own platforms and API, with open weights promised for November 4. Artificial Analysis scored it 55 on its Intelligence Index — fourth out of 215 tracked models — behind Claude Opus 5.5 at 58 and ahead of GPT-6 Astra at 53. The 11-point jump from the earlier K3 is the largest single-generation gain the lab has posted. Moonshot's self-reported Terminal-Bench 4.0 score is 65.7%, close to Opus 5.5's 66.4%; independent verification of the terminal-agent numbers is still pending. Pricing is set at $2 per million input tokens and $10 per million output tokens, roughly a third of Opus 5.5's list.

The release carries three signals worth separating from the usual benchmark theatre. First, the gap between the best Western frontier model and the best Chinese open-weight contender is now a single Intelligence Index point. Second, Moonshot is committing to publish weights on a hard date — November 4 — which, if honored, would make K3.1 Pro the strongest open-weight generalist available to anyone with the compute to run it. Third, pricing. If the public API numbers hold, Moonshot is undercutting Anthropic's flagship by roughly 3x on both input and output, which recalibrates the economics for any team that doesn't need Opus 5.5's specific agentic edge.

Context: the US federal ban on DeepSeek went into effect this month and DeepSeek's new $15B round, backed by Tencent and CATL, closed last week. Moonshot is now the second Chinese lab in two weeks to meaningfully close the frontier gap while expanding Chinese capital commitments. The Western pattern of 'closed-weights, premium-priced, API-only' no longer defines what the frontier looks like worldwide — and the open-weights pledge is what forces the question. There are also unresolved allegations that Moonshot paid influencers to promote the launch, which VentureBeat reported alongside the benchmark coverage; independent replication is still pending.

A note for learners: 'frontier model' is becoming a two-column spreadsheet. One column is closed, API-only, aligned with heavy safety tooling. The other is open-weight, globally downloadable, and priced to commoditize inference. The skills that matter are shifting with it: fine-tuning, local serving, and quantization are leaving the hobbyist corner and becoming production tools. If you only know how to call a hosted API, you now know half the stack.
